import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Erdős Problem 353

*References:*
- [erdosproblems.com/353](https://www.erdosproblems.com/353)
- [Er83d] Erdős, Paul, *Some combinatorial, geometric and set theoretic problems in measure
  theory*. Measure Theory, Oberwolfach 1983 (1984), 321-327.
- [Ko23] Kovač, V., *Coloring and density theorems for configurations of a given volume*.
  arXiv:2309.09973 (2023).
- [KoPr24] Kovač, V. and B. Predojević, *Polygons of unit area with vertices in sets of infinite
  planar measure*. arXiv:2412.11725 (2024).
- [Ko25] J. Koizumi, *Isosceles trapezoids of unit area with vertices in sets of infinite planar
  measure*. arXiv:2501.01914 (2025).
-/

open Affine EuclideanGeometry MeasureTheory

open scoped Real

namespace Erdos353

/--
Let $A\subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$ be a measurable set with infinite measure. Must $A$ contain the
vertices of an isosceles trapezoid of area $1$? What about an isosceles triangle, or a
right-angled triangle, or a cyclic quadrilateral, or a convex polygon with congruent sides?

Koizumi [Ko25] has resolved this question, proving that any set with infinite measure must
contain the vertices of an isosceles trapezoid, an isosceles triangle, and a right-angled
triangle, all of area $1$.

This statement formalizes the leading question, for isosceles trapezoids; the remaining
configurations are given as variants below. The area of a polygon is taken to be the Lebesgue
measure of the convex hull of its vertices.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 28 51, formal_proof using lean4 at "https://github.com/Jayyhk/erdos-lean/blob/110d489ed5c07e5b216453e092e9113127c98c9a/problems/353/Erdos353.lean"]
theorem erdos_353 : answer(True) ↔
    ∀ A : Set ℝ², MeasurableSet A → volume A = ⊤ →
      ∃ a ∈ A, ∃ b ∈ A, ∃ c ∈ A, ∃ d ∈ A,
        IsIsoscelesTrapezoid a b c d ∧
        volume (convexHull ℝ {a, b, c, d}) = 1 := by
  sorry

/--
Every measurable $A\subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$ with infinite measure contains the vertices of an
isosceles triangle of area $1$.

Koizumi [Ko25] has resolved this question, proving that any set with infinite measure must
contain the vertices of an isosceles trapezoid, an isosceles triangle, and a right-angled
triangle, all of area $1$.

Note the area condition forces `a`, `b`, `c` to be affinely independent, so no separate
non-degeneracy hypothesis is needed.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 28 51, formal_proof using lean4 at "https://github.com/Jayyhk/erdos-lean/blob/110d489ed5c07e5b216453e092e9113127c98c9a/problems/353/Erdos353.lean"]
theorem erdos_353.variants.isosceles_triangle :
    ∀ A : Set ℝ², MeasurableSet A → volume A = ⊤ →
      ∃ a ∈ A, ∃ b ∈ A, ∃ c ∈ A,
        IsIsosceles a b c ∧
        volume (convexHull ℝ {a, b, c}) = 1 := by
  sorry

/--
Every measurable $A\subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$ with infinite measure contains the vertices of a
right-angled triangle of area $1$.

Koizumi [Ko25] has resolved this question, proving that any set with infinite measure must
contain the vertices of an isosceles trapezoid, an isosceles triangle, and a right-angled
triangle, all of area $1$.

Note the area condition forces `a`, `b`, `c` to be affinely independent, so no separate
non-degeneracy hypothesis is needed.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 28 51, formal_proof using lean4 at "https://github.com/Jayyhk/erdos-lean/blob/110d489ed5c07e5b216453e092e9113127c98c9a/problems/353/Erdos353.lean"]
theorem erdos_353.variants.right_angled_triangle :
    ∀ A : Set ℝ², MeasurableSet A → volume A = ⊤ →
      ∃ a ∈ A, ∃ b ∈ A, ∃ c ∈ A,
        IsRightAngled a b c ∧
        volume (convexHull ℝ {a, b, c}) = 1 := by
  sorry

/--
Every measurable $A\subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$ with infinite measure contains the vertices of a
cyclic quadrilateral of area $1$.

Kovač and Predojević [KoPr24] have proved that this is true for cyclic quadrilaterals - that
is, every set with infinite measure contains four distinct points on a circle such that the
quadrilateral determined by these four points has area $1$. The quadrilateral determined by
four distinct concyclic points is their convex hull.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 28 51, formal_proof using lean4 at "https://github.com/Jayyhk/erdos-lean/blob/110d489ed5c07e5b216453e092e9113127c98c9a/problems/353/Erdos353.lean"]
theorem erdos_353.variants.cyclic_quadrilateral :
    ∀ A : Set ℝ², MeasurableSet A → volume A = ⊤ →
      ∃ Q : Set ℝ², Q ⊆ A ∧ Q.ncard = 4 ∧ Cospherical Q ∧
        volume (convexHull ℝ Q) = 1 := by
  sorry

/--
The answer is negative for convex polygons with congruent sides: Kovač and Predojević
[KoPr24] prove that there exists a set of infinite measure such that every convex polygon
with congruent sides and all vertices in the set has area $<1$.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 28 51, formal_proof using lean4 at "https://github.com/Jayyhk/erdos-lean/blob/110d489ed5c07e5b216453e092e9113127c98c9a/problems/353/Erdos353.lean"]
theorem erdos_353.variants.congruent_sides :
    ∃ A : Set ℝ², MeasurableSet A ∧ volume A = ⊤ ∧
      ∀ (n : ℕ) (v : Fin (n + 3) → ℝ²),
        IsCcwConvexPolygon v → (∀ i, v i ∈ A) →
        (∀ i, dist (v i) (v (i + 1)) = dist (v 0) (v 1)) →
        volume (convexHull ℝ (Set.range v)) < 1 := by
  sorry

end Erdos353

reformulations.difference: The trapezoid predicate uses strict convex order, parallel opposite sides, and equal diagonals rather than an explicit reflection-symmetry or equal-base-angle condition.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: For a strictly convex trapezoid, choose coordinates a=(-u,0), b=(u,0), c=(t+v,h), d=(t-v,h), with u,v>0 and h≠0. Equality of the squared diagonal lengths gives 4t(u+v)=0, hence t=0. This is exactly the reflection-symmetric isosceles trapezoid, and conversely symmetry gives equal diagonals. Unlike equal legs alone, this excludes nonrectangular parallelograms. The existentially chosen vertex order can be reversed without changing membership or convex-hull area. The coordinate calculation was checked in Lean, but the complete geometric normalization equivalence was not formalized.

reformulations.difference: There is no separate distinctness or affine-independence requirement on the three vertices.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: A collinear set's convex hull has zero two-dimensional Lebesgue measure. Consequently, the area-one condition implies AffineIndependent ℝ ![a,b,c], including pairwise distinctness. A pointwise equivalence between the displayed existential statement and the version adding affine independence was proved in scratch. Thus the degenerate cases admitted by IsIsosceles alone cannot witness this theorem.

reformulations.difference: IsRightAngled can hold on coincident points because Mathlib assigns angle π/2 when an incident vector is zero; the declaration nevertheless omits explicit nondegeneracy.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: The conjunction with convex-hull volume equal to 1 forces affine independence, so those default-angle cases are unreachable. The same Lean-proved existential equivalence adding affine independence applies to this triangle predicate. The three disjuncts cover precisely a right angle at any vertex, without imposing an axis direction.

reformulations.difference: The quadrilateral is represented by an unordered set Q satisfying Q.ncard = 4 and Cospherical Q.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Set.ncard_eq_four identifies this with exactly four pairwise distinct points; infinite sets have ncard 0 and cannot qualify. Cospherical means equidistance from a center, and four distinct points force the radius to be strictly positive. Four distinct points on a circle are in convex position, and their convex hull is the quadrilateral whose area the source specifies. The four-point existential equivalence and the positive-radius equivalence were proved in Lean.

reformulations.difference: The universal polygon quantifier fixes one orientation through IsCcwConvexPolygon and indexes vertices by Fin (n + 3).
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Every polygon with at least three vertices has one of the two cyclic orientations. Reversal i ↦ -i preserves the vertex set, membership in A, every side length, and convex-hull area. In scratch, the entire universal polygon property was proved equivalent to the version using IsConvexPolygon, which admits either orientation. The indices n+3 cover all sizes at least three, and Fin addition includes the closing edge; evaluations gave [1,2,0] and [1,2,3,0]. Strict convexity also forces the common side length to be positive.

reformulations.difference: MeasurableSet on the chosen Euclidean space means Borel measurability, whereas the papers use Lebesgue measurability.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Every Lebesgue-measurable set contains a Borel subset equal to it almost everywhere, hence of the same infinite measure. The four positive configuration-existence properties pass from subsets to supersets; the negative polygon-area property passes to subsets. Therefore the Borel and completed-Lebesgue formulations are equivalent for all five declarations. Generic equivalences for these monotone and antitone properties were proved using NullMeasurableSet.exists_measurable_subset_ae_eq and measure_congr.

review.notes: All five statements agree with the cited problem and its recorded solutions. In particular, congruent_sides states Kovač–Predojević's stronger counterexample theorem, not merely the negation of an existence question. The tests and equivalences in /workspace/review/scratch.lean and /workspace/review/trapezoid_checks.lean compile; their checked lemmas use only propext, Classical.choice, and Quot.sound, not the problem's sorry declarations. The linked external proof source contains matching statements for all five results and no sorry, admit, or custom axioms. However, rebuilding that standalone source against the sandbox's Lean 4.33.1/Mathlib failed with elaboration/API compatibility errors, and its original pinned environment was unavailable. Thus the external proof was inspected but not independently kernel-verified; this is not evidence of a mathematical or status defect.
